lines.text: What does a software team {q}actually produce?
In {y}1985, Peter Naur's {ans}surprising answer: {notcode}not the code.
Programming, he argued, is {tb}theory building: working out how {world}part of the world will be handled by a {prog}program.
{sec}Code and documents, even {specs}specs, come second.
It's theory in {ryle}Gilbert Ryle's sense: {how}knowing how, and {explain}being able to explain it.
Whoever holds it can {map}map the program to the world, {justify}justify each part, and {adapt}judge which changes fit.
Naur saw successive teams {inherit}inherit a compiler, {docs}with full code and full docs, and still {patch}patch its design apart.
{notravel}The theory didn't travel.
And when its holders {leave}leave, a program {dies}dies, even {runs}while it still runs.
Now {agents}agents write the code.
Text is {free}nearly free. But for Naur, {never}text was never the expensive part. {theory}The theory is.
And {specify}specifying is how you build it.
The agent {getsspec}gets your spec. {keep}You keep the theory.
In a {reg}regulated enterprise, that theory is {scattered}scattered: {rule}a rule buried in policy, {quirk}a platform quirk one engineer knows, {unsaid}a constraint nobody says out loud.
{rgtb}Requirements gathering is theory building.
So: {t1}trace every requirement to its source.
{t2}Write down the why, and {rejected}what you rejected.
{t3}Rehearse change: does a new rule {fit}fit, or {patch}need a patch?
And {t4}sit with the people who hold the theory. {loop}Keep them in the loop as agents build.
{c1}Code is the output. {c2}The spec is the handoff. {c3}The theory is the product.
